title: Test out of Part A
crib:
You don't need R experience for this test. These are the behaviours it
relies on. If another language already works this way, you can answer
from what you know; where R differs, this sheet tells you.

- **Counting starts at 1.** `x[1]` is the first value, `x[2]` the second.
  (Python and JavaScript count from 0.)
- **Storing:** `x <- 5` stores 5 in `x`. A plain `=` does the same at the
  top level.
- **Testing for equality:** `==` asks whether two things are equal. `!=`
  asks whether they differ.
- **Text** goes in quotes, so `"142"` is text, not a number.
- **TRUE and FALSE** are capitalised, and adding them up counts the TRUEs.
- **Missing values** are written `NA`. Arithmetic and comparisons with `NA`
  give `NA`, not `FALSE` or zero. Summaries such as `mean()` give `NA` too,
  unless you add `na.rm = TRUE`, which leaves missing values out.
- **`round()`** rounds halves to the nearest *even* number, so
  `round(2.5)` is 2.
- **Functions** take arguments in brackets. Some arguments have a default
  value, used if you don't give one.
- **`c()`** joins values into a vector.
- **Filtering:** `x[condition]` keeps only the values where the condition
  is TRUE.

options.feedback:
Right. Multiplication happens before addition, as it does in
school arithmetic.

That's working left to right. R follows the usual order: `3 * 4`
first, then the `2` is added.

That's adding first. The `*` binds tighter than the `+`, so `3 * 4`
happens first.

That treats the `*` as if it were a `+`. It multiplies `3` by `4`,
then adds.

items.title: Storing and replacing
items.prompt:
```r
sbp <- 142
sbp <- sbp + 10
```

What is `sbp` now?

options.feedback:
Right. The second line reads `sbp`, adds 10, and stores the result
back into `sbp`. The old value is replaced.

The second line changes `sbp`. It reads the old 142, adds 10, and
stores 152 in the same name.
That's only the amount added. The result, 152, is what gets stored.

Storing into a name that already exists replaces its value. Only one
value is kept.

The quotes make `"142"` text. R won't do arithmetic on text, even
text that looks like a number.
R doesn't join the two. It refuses to add text to a number.

`NA` is R's marker for a missing value. Nothing is missing here: the
problem is that `"142"` is text, so R stops with an error.

Right. The quotes make `"142"` text, and R won't do arithmetic on
text. The error names the problem.

items.title: Adding up TRUEs
items.prompt:
What does this give?

```r
sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))
```

options.feedback:
Right. TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, so the total is 2. This is
how you count how many values meet a condition.
Each TRUE counts as 1, and there are two of them.
There are three values, but FALSE counts as 0, not 1.

options.text: An error — you can't add TRUE
options.feedback: You can. R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0 when you add them.

items.title: Testing for equality
items.prompt: Which line checks whether `sbp` is equal to 142?

options.feedback:
Right. `==` asks whether two things are equal. It gives TRUE or FALSE
and doesn't change `sbp`.

At the top level, a plain `=` stores 142 in `sbp`, the same as `<-`.
It doesn't test anything.
That stores 142 in `sbp`. It doesn't ask a question.
`!=` asks whether the two are *different*. That's the opposite.

items.title: A default you didn't ask for

options.feedback:
Right. `round()` has a default for how many decimal places, and that
default is 0. You didn't give it one, so R rounds to a whole number.

That's one decimal place. You didn't ask for one; the default is zero
places.
That's not a rounding of 2.567 to any number of places.
2.567 is closer to 3 than to 2 when rounded to a whole number.

Many people expect this, and many languages give it. R rounds a
half to the nearest even whole number, so 2.5 becomes 2.

Right. R rounds halves to the nearest even number: `round(2.5)` is 2
and `round(3.5)` is 4. It's worth knowing when you're rounding
lab values.
Nothing has been rounded, so the decimal stays.

No error. Rounding a half is allowed; it just rounds to an even
number.

That's the first value. R counts positions from 1, so `bp[2]` is
the second.

Right. R counts positions from 1, so `bp[2]` is the second value.
Python and JavaScript count from 0, so there `[2]` would be the
third value. That difference catches people switching languages.

That's the third value. In R, the second value is `bp[2]`, because
counting starts at 1.
There is. Position 2 exists, and it holds 142.

Right. `bp > 140` gives one TRUE or FALSE per value, and `bp[...]`
keeps the values where it's TRUE.

That's the comparison on its own. Putting it in square brackets
keeps the values where it's TRUE.

Nothing has been filtered out. Every value would have to pass the test
to appear here.
156 is also above 140, so it's kept as well.

items.title: One missing value spoils the mean
items.prompt:
What does this give?

```r
mean(c(118, NA, 131))
```

options.feedback:
Right. `mean()` won't guess at a missing value, so the whole result
is `NA`. You have to decide what to do about it.

That's the mean of the two readings you do have. `mean()` doesn't
leave the missing one out unless you ask it to.

A missing value isn't a zero. `mean()` gives `NA` when a value is
missing.

No error. `mean()` gives `NA`, which is R's way of saying the result
can't be known from this data.

items.title: Leaving the missing one out
items.prompt:
What does this give?

```r
mean(c(118, NA, 131), na.rm = TRUE)
```

options.feedback:
Right. `na.rm = TRUE` leaves the missing value out, so the mean is
of 118 and 131.

That's the result without `na.rm = TRUE`. With it, the missing value
is dropped.

That's the total of the two readings, not their mean. Dividing by
two gives 124.5.

Nothing has been turned into zero. The missing value is left out, and
the mean of the other two is returned.

items.title: A missing value is not a zero

options.feedback:
Right. R doesn't know what the missing value is, so it can't say
whether it equals 0. The answer is missing too. To test for a missing
value, use `is.na()`.

Tempting, but `NA` isn't a number that's different from zero. R
doesn't know its value, so it can't say it's not zero.

`NA` isn't 0, so it can't be equal to 0. R goes further and says the
answer is unknown.

The comparison gives a TRUE/FALSE-style answer, which here is `NA`,
not a number.
